blocks.heading: Qualities of a good manager
blocks.text: Useful managerial qualities include clear communication, sound judgement, integrity, fairness, confidence, willingness to listen and the ability to organise and adapt. Communication makes responsibilities and instructions understandable. Judgement weighs relevant evidence before acting. Integrity supports trust because staff and suppliers can rely on truthful information. Fairness can help cooperation when allocating work or handling disputes. Confidence should be paired with listening rather than treating every challenge as disloyalty. Adaptability matters when a plan no longer fits the facts. A quality describes how capable a manager is; a function describes the management activity being performed. Naming planning and controlling does not by itself identify personal qualities. Support a quality with its business effect rather than claiming that a pleasant personality automatically achieves objectives.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omu Repairs’ manager listens when technicians warn that a promised deadline is unsafe, checks the evidence and communicates a realistic revised plan to the customer. Listening, judgement and integrity are qualities shown by the response. Revising the schedule is planning and explaining the priorities supports leading. Distinguishing qualities from functions makes the description precise.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain the difference between the two descriptions of fictional manager Nela: “she is honest and listens carefully” and “she plans output and checks results”.

Honesty and listening are managerial qualities: attributes affecting how she manages. Planning and controlling are functions: activities she performs. The qualities can improve those functions, for example honest reporting supports useful control, but naming a function does not identify a personal quality.
